JOINT STATEMENT AND SIGNATURE PAGE

The Government of Georgia and the UN Country Team in Georgia reaffirm their shared commitment to
forge a dynamic partnership that will drive progress towards. Georgia's national development priorities and
the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Together, we pledge to.work for the benefit of the people
of Georgia to foster. an inclusive, prosperous, and sustainable future where every person can reach their full
potential.

Building on the success of our past cooperation, the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation
Framework (from. now.on. UN. Cooperation. Framework) will guide the work of the UN development system
agencies in Georgia between 2026 and 2030.

The Government's and UN's. joint efforts. will be guided. by. the principles. of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable.
Development, emphasizing. national. ownership, transparency, and. mutual. respect.

In signing. hereafter, the Government of Georgia and members of the United. Nations Country Team, endorse
the UN Cooperation Framework and underscore their joint commitment towards the achievement of its.
results.

GEORGIA

The 2026-2030 United Nations Sustainable
Development Cooperation Framework for

Georgia sets out the strategic vision.and collective
commitment of the UN system to support the
country’s sustainable development priorities in
alignment with the 2030 Agenda. It is the result of a
comprehensive and inclusive design process, co-led
by the Government of Georgia and. the UN. Country,
Team, and informed. by extensive.consultations. with.
civil society, academia, youth, private sector, and
development partners.

Georgia has. made notable progress as.an.upper-
middle-income country, with. strong economic.
growth, expanded universal healthcare, and
significant investments.in. green energy.and
education. However, persistent challenges remain,
including the urban-rural divide, demographic
decline, youth. unemployment, gender. inequality,
vulnerability to climate change, and unresolved
conflict that severely. affects. the people in Abkhazia,
Georgia and the Tskhinvali. Region/South. Ossetia,
Georgia. These complex and interlinked issues.
require integrated and transformative solutions to
ensure inclusive and sustainable development.

The Cooperation Framework was developed
through a participatory and iterative process,
grounded in a comprehensive Country. Analysis
and guided by systems thinking and foresight
methodologies. The overarching Theory of Change
identifies. four. interconnected. pathways for. change:

1. Inclusive Growth and Green Transition

2. Human Development through Education,
Health, and Social Protection

3. Governance, Human Rights, Gender. Equality,
and. Social Cohesion

4. An Enabling Environment for Peace

These pathways are underpinned. by. the UN's. global
programming principles: leaving. no.one behind,
human rights-based approach, gender equality and
women’s empowerment, resilience, sustainability,
and. accountability. Cross-cutting themes include
youth empowerment, human mobility, and digital
transformation.

The UN system commits to contributing to these
change pathways through the following outcomes:

Outcome 1: By.2030, people in Georgia, especially
those living in rural. areas, benefit from.a growing,
more diversified, green. and inclusive economy,.and
a healthier environment more resilient to climate
change and natural hazards.

UN contributions include support for competitive
MSMEs.development, inclusive labour markets.and
rural economies, climate resilient and risk informed
development, agri-food. systems, environmental
governance, digital innovation, improved
connectivity and. deeper value chains.

Outcome 2: By 2030, people in Georgia enjoy.
improved learning outcomes, healthier lives

and. reduced. vulnerabilities, supported by.
comprehensive social. protection, thereby. bridging.
the rural-urban divide.

The UN will focus.on inclusive education. systems,
universal health coverage, mental health, and
comprehensive social protection.across. the life
cycle.

Outcome 3: By 2030, people in Georgia benefit
from.a more decentralized and inclusive
governance system, with. stronger. human rights.
protections, gender equality, and enhanced social.
cohesion.

The UN aims to strengthen human rights
institutions, gender. equality. mechanisms, civic
space,.and. participatory. governance.

Outcome 4: By. 2030, people affected by conflict,
including IDPs, enjoy enhanced. engagement, trust,
and resilience for an enabling environment for.
peace, across. dividing lines.

UN's contributions include expanding dialogue
platforms, enhancing. access.to services and
livelihoods, and protecting human rights across
dividing lines.

by a Joint National-UN Steering Committee
(JSC), co-chaired. by the Prime Minister. or. senior.

GEORGIA

The present Cooperation Framework has been
informed. by comprehensive analyses of the
situation. for. sustainable development in.Georgia.
conducted by the Government and independently
by the UN. It is broadly. aligned. with the
Government's Vision. 2030. development strategy
and the 2025-2028 Government Programme. This
chapter draws on. those reports.to highlight notable
key.achievements.and challenges.’ As.a.fast-
growing upper-middle-income country, Georgia
has made significant progress towards sustainable
development and the 2030 Agenda. For example,
poverty. rates have been reduced, universal
healthcare has. expanded, and.investments in
green energy infrastructure have increased. These
achievements were realized despite external
challenges such as. the COVID-19 pandemic and
geopolitical uncertainty, not least due to. the
ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. GDP. growth hit a
decade-high 11%.in. 2022 and remained strong
through 2025. Coupled. with social. policies, this
contributed to.a fall in the national poverty rate.
from. 37% in.2010.to. less than 10% in 2024, while
extreme poverty dropped from. over 23% to less
than 6%. by 2023 according to the World Bank’s
definition. Inequality,.as. measured by the Gini
coefficient, has. also. trended. downward. overall. The
pension reform established a universal pillar for old-
age income security. and contributed to. the decline
in. poverty.

Georgia also. showed notable social development
improvements in. health and education. The infant
mortality rate decreased by 69% between 2000 and
2023, largely. thanks to. expanded immunization,
with a 94% coverage rate of the routine childhood
vaccination programme. The maternal mortality.
ratio.has stood. at around 25.per 100,000.live
births. on. average over the past decade, double
the European average of 13. Primary and secondary

school enrolment was sustained at high levels,
and large-scale initiatives were launched to
improve. educational infrastructure, for. example.
rehabilitating 800 schools by 2026. Public spending
on education stood at 3.8% of GDP in 2022, up
from. only 2% in the early. 2000s, but short of the
EU. average of 5% and of the stated policy target
to. reach. 6% by. 2030. Universal. health coverage.
has. been. established and expanded, improving
access to quality healthcare. In early 2025,
Georgia achieved a. public health milestone by
being. declared malaria-free by WHO, and it has
earned. international recognition. for its. hepatitis-C
elimination. programme.

Georgia has set ambitious targets for climate action
and.environmental sustainability. It committed to
carbon neutrality. by 2050 - with a roadmap for.
implementation. enshrined. in. the Long-Term. Low-
Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS).- and
expanded protected natural areas. with the aim

to protect 25% of ecosystems by 2030. Georgia's
unique Colchic rainforests and wetlands. were
inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021,
reflecting. efforts to. safeguard. biodiversity.

Reforms have been. launched in. public
administration, decentralization, education,

and other areas. Georgia has cooperated with
international human rights mechanisms and
adopted the 2022-2030 National Human Rights.
Strategy. The Public. Defender. enjoys. top “A-status”
accreditation. since 2018. The 17. Sustainable.
Development Goals (SDGs) have been integrated
into national policy. documents, including at the
municipal level.

Overall, Georgia's. progress on. specific SDG
Indicators. shows. significant advancements in
several areas, notably health (SDG 3); affordable

and clean energy. (SDG 7); decent work and
economic growth (SDG 8); industry, innovation
and infrastructure (SDG 9), and partnerships.

for the goals (SDG 17). More limited results

have been achieved in gender.equality. (SDG 5);
reduced inequalities (SDG 10); sustainable cities
and communities (SDG 11); and responsible
consumption and. production. (SDG 12). For.many.
SDG targets, there is insufficient data to. evaluate
progress.

Notwithstanding these achievements, significant
development challenges. persist. The enduring.
urban-rural divide is.a. deeply. rooted structural
challenge in Georgia which cuts across almost

all aspects of sustainable development. Rural
towns. and communities lag behind urban
centres.in.access.to. quality. education, healthcare,
infrastructure, and.economic. opportunities.
Poverty. is higher in. rural areas, while labour.

force participation. rates are. lower, and. many.
rural. households rely on subsistence farming

and social transfers. While absolute poverty has
declined overall, relative poverty remains.almost
stagnant at around 20% of the population,
although it. has fallen slightly in recent years. In
fact, for. the poorest rural households, relative
poverty. rates have even increased, highlighting
how. geographic inequality. and social.exclusion
overlap. Children. are especially vulnerable as.seen
in the child. poverty. rate which has stood. about
10. percentage points. higher than. the rate among
pensioners, although the gap has narrowed in
recent years to a little over 5 percentage points in
2024. Many. workers. remain in. the informal sector,
not least women. in. the care economy. While the
social. protection. system. has. been. expanded, it.
remains relatively. fragmented, does. not provide
integrated life-cycle support, and largely excludes
informal workers. Policies that promote inclusive
development are needed to overcome this divide
and live up to the promise of leaving no one
behind. Such reforms also. have the potential to.
reduce the risk of the.’middle-income. trap’ by.

GEORGIA

promoting long-term human capital development
and. productivity growth.

Upgrading transport and energy connectivity has
emerged as one of the central themes of economic
development in the South Caucasus, and Georgia's
geographic position. along. the Middle Corridor.
creates strategic opportunities for. infrastructure
investments that can be leveraged for SDG
acceleration. The full realization of the potential will
require efforts to reduce bottlenecks, expand trade
infrastructure, and strengthen soft connectivity.
through more integrated.and streamlined trade and
customs facilitation, intermodal transport solutions,
and international. regulatory. harmonization.

Energy. connectivity is another. key priority, with

the flagship Black Sea Submarine Cable poised to
connect the South.Caucasus with. the European
electricity market, increasing the export potential
for. renewable energy. in the whole region.

The ambitious goals for climate and environmental
policy. require urgent. implementation. measures:
stronger disaster risk reduction, climate-resilient
infrastructure, and sustainable natural resource
management are needed to. protect communities
- especially. rural and mountain populations -
from climate shocks and can also foster the green
transition. by creating. new. economic. opportunities.
Environmental issues like air pollution and
deforestation also pose health and livelihood risks.
Itis important to. equip workers, communities and
authorities with the right skills for this transition to
fully realize this strategic opportunity.

Georgia also faces the need to strengthen its
demographic resilience. Its population. has.

been shrinking due to emigration and low birth
rates, resulting. in.a rapidly ageing society. Over.
160,000 citizens of Georgia emigrated in 2023
alone - especially youth and. working-age adults -
depleting the skilled workforce and contributing
to. labour shortages. Meanwhile, net migration. has.
been offset by significant immigration in recent


 
GEORGIA

years, bringing opportunities for economic renewal
and presenting considerations for integration

and social. cohesion. At the same time, youth
unemployment and inactivity remain problematic:
roughly. one in four. young, people (aged. 15-29)

is neither. in education, employment, nor training
(NEETs). There is a gender gap that increases

with. age: in the 15-24 cohort, men and. women

are equally likely to. be in this, category (17.5%.

each in 2024), while in the 15-29 cohort, 27% of
women are in this category compared to. 21% of
men. Educational outcomes lag significantly - a
majority. of 15-year-olds fail basic proficiency. in
reading, math and science, per PISA test results.
This combination of emigration, skills mismatch,
and limited. opportunities for youth threatens
future growth and social stability. Strengthening.
human capital through better education.and job
opportunities. is an urgent need. Youth. engagement
needs to be integrated across thematic areas.

Gender inequality. persists in the labour market
and in both public and private life. Women’s labour.
force participation (about 45%) is far below men’s
(66%), due in part to.care responsibilities and social
norms limiting women’s opportunities, especially.
in. rural areas and.among ethnic minorities. In
2024, the unadjusted. monthly pay. gap for women
was. 32% less. pay. than. for. men, whereas the pay.
gap. adjusted for demographic factors like age and
location stood at 21%. While Georgia has ratified
most core human rights.conventions.

and adopted legal strategies to address this

issue, entrenched social norms, as well as limited
childcare and family. support continue to restrict

women’s empowerment. Additionally, persons
with. disabilities.and. minority groups.face barriers
in access to services and employment, often
exacerbated by insufficient data and analysis

of their needs, and societal attitudes that may.
stigmatize persons with disabilities.

Georgia. was. granted. EU. candidacy status.

by the European Council in December 2023.
Recent years. saw heightened political tensions,
which risk diverting attention from reforms and
pose a challenge for sustainable development.
Decentralization has. brought tangible results. since
the reform started, although. local governments.
often lack capacity and. resources .to.deliver services
equally across municipalities. The situation in

and around Abkhazia, Georgia and the Tskhinvali
Region/South. Ossetia, Georgia, continues to. pose
political, military and. security. risks. Conflict-affected.
people remain vulnerable and marginalized due to
the unresolved conflict.

All these. challenges. are highly. interlinked. and.
mutually. reinforcing. For example, bridging
the urban-rural gap will contribute to. poverty.
reduction. and. gender. equality. by bringing.
services and jobs closer to those left behind,
while green transition efforts can create new
economic opportunities. in rural regions. By.
pursuing. inclusive economic growth, social
equity, effective. governance, environmental
sustainability, and youth empowerment,
Georgia's policymakers and UN partners aim to
accelerate progress on all dimensions of the 2030
Agenda.

GEORGIA

The UN Sustainable Development Cooperation
Framework is the central planning and
implementation. tool. guiding.the UN’s. development
work in each country in which the UN operates.

It aligns UN support with national priorities

and the 2030 Agenda, serving as a strategic,
results-based partnership framework co-created
with government and other. stakeholders. As.a
cornerstone of UN.development system reform,
the Cooperation Framework enhances coherence,
accountability, and impact by. unifying. efforts of.
various. UN Development System entities. under.

a single strategy. At the country. level, it is.a. vital
tool for inclusive planning, resource mobilization,
and monitoring progress toward sustainable
development, while remaining adaptable to
emerging challenges.

This Cooperation, Framework was jointly.
developed through extensive consultations with
the Government of Georgia.and other. national
stakeholders, aligned to the country’s national
priorities. The independent evaluation of the
2021-2025 Cooperation Framework underlined
the importance of revitalizing the UN position and
achieving greater strategic focus and embracing
innovation, strengthening, private sector
engagement, and fostering greater inclusivity.
These recommendations guided the strategic
prioritization process, and the design of the results
framework of this Cooperation Framework.

Inclusivity. characterized. this planning. process.
from the outset. The document was co-created

in. an.iterative process by the UN Country. Team
(UNCT) in Georgia and the Government of Georgia,
through the guidance. and overall coordination of.
the Administration of the Government. .The private
sector, civil society, social partners, academia, youth
groups, and international development partners
were also. engaged in. participatory. sessions, where
initial planned results for UN contribution were
shared and. discussed. These sessions, confirmed
the relevance of the results. pursued. under.

the Cooperation Framework and provided an
opportunity to explore potential partnerships and
synergies. across stakeholders’ groups.

2.1. FROM COUNTRY ANALYSIS TO
COOPERATION. FRAMEWORK PRIORITIES

The UNCT, with support from. the wider. UN
Development System, conducted a comprehensive
Country. Analysis.as part of its strategic planning
process leading up to the design of this
Cooperation Framework. The Country. Analysis
aimed to identify. the most important constraints.
in following a sustainable development path from
the perspective of Georgia's national development
ambitions and. of the normative standards to
which Georgia has committed as a UN member
state, including the 2030. Agenda and. its. SDGs..
The key focus of the analysis. was to enhance the
understanding. of the integrated and. interlinked
nature of all areas. of sustainable development
through the application of systems thinking.and
foresight methodologies. The analysis. identified
five main themes that can drive change and offer.
potential solutions to existing challenges:

1. Inclusive economic development as.a driver for
human capital development

2. Overcoming the urban-rural divide to. promote
inclusive growth

3. Good.governance. and human rights for.a.
peaceful. and inclusive society

4. Agreen and just transition for climate
adaptation and resilience

5. Ensuring a promising future for. Georgia’s youth.

In.early. April. 2025, the UNCT. convened. a
strategic planning retreat to. define the UN’s
positioning and prioritize solutions emerging
from.the Country Analysis. This retreat served
as a pivotal moment for reflection and strategic
alignment,.as participants. assessed the UN
system’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities,

and threats in relation to. Georgia's sustainable
development goals. The development solutions
were evaluated. through two. critical lenses: 1)
their transformational potential to drive deep,
systemic, and sustainable change aligned

with national priorities and the SDGs; and 2)
their alignment with the six guiding principles
underpinning. all. UN. work. on. sustainable
development: leaving.no one. behind. (LNOB),;. the
human rights-based approach (HRBA); gender
equality.and women’s.empowerment (GEWE);
resilience to.shocks such as. natural disasters,
conflict, pandemics, and price fluctuations;
sustainability. through the. strengthening

of capacities of national and sub-national
institutions; and. accountability for achieving. the
goals.

As. the. next fundamental step. in this. prioritization
process, the UN engaged in a series of
consultations. with the Government of Georgia
to define the four actionable priorities for future
UN. development support to the country. Further
consultations. with civil society. organizations,
social partners, private sector actors, academia,
youth groups and. international development
partners, played a crucial. role.in validating.and
enriching the proposed areas of work. These
dialogues helped to validate the UN's strategic
planning direction and ensured that the
proposed Cooperation Framework is inclusive,
responsive, and. reflective of a broad. spectrum
of stakeholder insights. At the same time, these
consultations highlighted the need to integrate
systematically a multitude of perspectives on
sustainable development to scale up initiatives,
achieve results with. strategic. impact, and. foster.
stronger partnerships, including. on financing. for.
development.

This comprehensive consultative process guided
the UN in the definition of the four outcomes of this
Cooperation Framework and UN's contributions to.
the realization of the outcomes.

2.2. THEORY. OF. CHANGE FOR THE
COOPERATION. FRAMEWORK PRIORITIES

Georgia's transition to an upper middle-income
country, characterized by robust and capable
institutions, a growing economy, and. reduced
reliance on international development assistance,
calls for.a strategic shift of the UN value proposition
in Georgia. towards key. reform. advisory services,
enhanced knowledge management, and

stronger transformational partnerships with both
governmental and non-governmental stakeholders.
As highlighted. in. the evaluation of the 2021-

2025 Cooperation Framework, the impact of UN's.
development support could be strengthened by.
better alignment of its strategic focus. with Georgia's
economic growth trajectory, strengthening
partnerships with the private sector, embracing
innovation, and. promoting. greater.inclusion.

These considerations. guided the identification of
the solution pathways for UN contributions under.
this Cooperation Framework, under the overarching
objective of reducing the rural-urban divide,
through inclusive, green development.

The overall. theory. of change. for. Georgia's.
progress towards the SDGs is premised on. the
interconnectedness.of the main. components of.
the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development,
and.more specifically People, Prosperity, Planet,
Partnership, and Peace. Recognizing that
sustainable economic growth is. inseparable from
environmental protection and climate action, this
Framework positions these priorities as. a unified
and essential pillar. of its theory of change. It
embraces. green. growth not only.as a necessity. but
as.a powerful opportunity. to, create decent work
and sustainable livelihoods. By integrating climate
considerations into economic planning, Georgia
can enhance its resilience, unlock new.economic
opportunities, and responsibly harness its. natural
resources with. future generations in. mind. This.
approach also paves the way for. revitalizing. rural
